title: Atorvastatin
wiki_lead:
Atorvastatin, sold under the brand name Lipitor among others, is a statin medication used to prevent cardiovascular disease in those at high risk and to treat abnormal lipid levels. For the prevention of cardiovascular disease, statins are a first-line treatment in reducing cholesterol. It is taken by mouth.
Common side effects may include diarrhea, heartburn, nausea, muscle pain (typically mild and dose-dependent) and, less frequently, joint pain. Muscle symptoms often occur during the first year and are commonly influenced by pre-existing health issues and the nocebo effect. Most patients can continue therapy with dose adjustment or statin switching. Rare (<0.1%) but serious side effects may include rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle disorder), liver problems and diabetes. Use during pregnancy may harm the fetus. Like all statins, atorvastatin works by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme found in the liver that plays a role in producing cholesterol.
Atorvastatin was patented in 1986 and approved for medical use in the United States in 1996. It is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. It is available as a generic medication. In 2024, it was the most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 115 million prescriptions. In Australia, in 2023, it was the second most prescribed medication after Rosuvastatin.

Medical uses
The primary uses of atorvastatin are for the treatment of dyslipidemia and for the prevention of cardiovascular disease.


Dyslipidemia
Hypercholesterolemia (heterozygous familial and nonfamilial) and mixed dyslipidemia (Fredrickson types IIa and IIb) to reduce total cholesterol, LDL-C, apo-B, triglycerides levels, and CRP as well as increase HDL levels
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in children
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
Hypertriglyceridemia (Fredrickson Type IV)
Primary dysbetalipoproteinemia (Fredrickson Type III)
Combined hyperlipidemia


Cardiovascular disease
Primary prevention of heart attack, stroke, and need for revascularization procedures in people who have risk factors such as age, smoking, high blood pressure, low HDL-C, and a family history of early heart disease, but have not yet developed evidence of coronary artery disease.
Secondary prevention of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, major coronary events, ischaemic heart disease and revascularization in people with established coronary artery disease. The effect is dose-dependent and is amplified at higher doses. Close monitoring of liver function tests is required when high doses are used
Alongside other lifestyle changes in primary and secondary prevention of angina
Myocardial infarction and stroke prevention in people with type 2 diabetes

grok_lead:
Atorvastatin is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent and selective competitive inhibitor of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A ( HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis, primarily used to manage dyslipidemias by reducing low-density lipoprotein ( LDL) cholesterol levels and to prevent cardiovascular disease. By decreasing hepatic cholesterol production, atorvastatin upregulates LDL receptors on liver cells, enhancing clearance of LDL from plasma and thereby lowering circulating cholesterol concentrations. First synthesized in 1985 by Bruce Roth at Warner-Lambert (later acquired by Pfizer), atorvastatin was developed into the blockbuster drug Lipitor, approved by the FDA in 1996 and launched in 1997, eventually generating over $125 billion in sales due to its potency in LDL reduction compared to earlier statins. In the United States, brand-name Lipitor (atorvastatin calcium) is now marketed by Viatris Specialty LLC, after the product rights were transferred from Pfizer following the 2020 spin-off of its Upjohn division into Viatris (merged with Mylan). Pfizer retains historical association as the original developer and marketer through its acquisition of Warner-Lambert.
The U.S. patent for Lipitor expired in June 2011, leading to the entry of generic atorvastatin versions starting November 30, 2011. Brand-name Lipitor continues under Viatris in the U.S.
In 2023, atorvastatin (including generics and brands like Lipitor and Atorvaliq) remained the most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 115 million prescriptions filled for over 29 million people, underscoring its widespread use in lipid management and cardiovascular prevention. Large-scale randomized trials, such as the Collaborative Atorvastatin Diabetes Study (CARDS) and Anglo-Scandinavian Cardiac Outcomes Trial-Lipid Lowering Arm (ASCOT-LLA), have shown that atorvastatin reduces the risk of major cardiovascular events by 16-37% relative to placebo or less intensive therapy, particularly in high-risk groups like those with type 2 diabetes or multiple risk factors, though absolute risk reductions in primary prevention remain modest for low-risk individuals. Despite these benefits, atorvastatin's use has faced scrutiny over adverse effects, including myalgia affecting up to 10-15% of users, rare rhabdomyolysis, and a small increase in new-onset diabetes risk, prompting ongoing debate about overprescription in primary prevention where empirical evidence of net benefit is weaker and patient-reported harms may be underappreciated in clinical guidelines.
